title: 22. Interview: Data Archiving
summary: Interview Q&A for Data Archiving — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Data Archiving interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is the difference between backup, archive, and cold storage?
**Answer:** A **backup** is a copy of active data kept for disaster recovery — it is restored when the primary is lost, the goal is to get back to operational state quickly, and backups are typically overwritten on a rolling schedule (daily incremental, weekly full, retain 30 days). An **archive** is the primary copy of inactive data that has been removed from the active system — the goal is long-term retention for compliance or rare retrieval, not disaster recovery. Archives are written once, indexed, and held for years. **Cold storage** is the storage medium (Glacier, Azure Archive) that archives live on — it is the cheap, slow tier. The relationship: an archive is what you keep (a logical concept), cold storage is where you keep it (a physical/tier concept), and a backup is a separate operational copy of active data. A common mistake is conflating backups and archives — using backup software for compliance retention leads to data loss when the backup rotation ages off records that regulation required you to keep. The right design: backups on hot/warm tiers with rolling retention for DR, archives on cold tiers with fixed retention for compliance, and clear metadata distinguishing the two.
**Visual:**
```
Backup:    copy of ACTIVE data, rolling retention (30d), restored on DR
Archive:   PRIMARY copy of INACTIVE data, fixed retention (7yr), rare retrieval
Cold:      the storage TIER (Glacier, Azure Archive) where archives live
practice:  backup on hot/warm (fast restore), archive on cold (cheap retention)
```

### Q2. How do S3 lifecycle policies work, and how do you design them?
**Answer:** An S3 lifecycle policy is a set of rules attached to a bucket or prefix that automatically transitions objects between storage classes or deletes them based on age. Each rule has a `transition` action with `Days` (minimum age in days) and `StorageClass` (target tier), and optionally an `expiration` action with `Days` for deletion. Rules apply per-object, evaluated by S3 daily. A typical pattern for log data: `Standard -> Standard-IA at 30d -> Glacier Instant at 60d -> Glacier Deep at 180d -> expire at 365d`. Design principles: (1) **Match the access decay curve** — if 80% of access is in the first 30 days, transition to IA at 30d; if access decays slowly, transition later to avoid paying IA's per-GB retrieval fee on frequent access. (2) **Mind minimum durations** — Standard-IA has a 30-day minimum, Glacier Flexible 90-day, Glacier Deep 180-day; deleting before incurs prorated charges. (3) **Use prefix scoping** — apply different policies per prefix (`logs/`, `media/`, `backups/`) rather than one bucket-wide rule. (4) **Versioning matters** — for versioned buckets, rules apply to non-current versions separately; common pattern is to delete old versions after 90 days. (5) **Monitor with S3 Storage Lens** to verify the policy is actually moving data as expected. Anti-pattern: one giant bucket with no policy — costs balloon as data accumulates indefinitely on Standard.
**Visual:**
```
rule:    {prefix: "logs/", transitions: [(30d, IA), (60d, Glacier), (180d, Deep)],
          expiration: 365d}
match access decay curve, mind min durations (IA 30d, Glacier 90d, Deep 180d)
scope per prefix, versioned buckets -> separate rules for non-current versions
monitor: S3 Storage Lens shows tier distribution and savings
```

### Q3. What is WORM storage, and why is it required for compliance?
**Answer:** WORM (Write Once Read Many) is a storage model where data, once written, cannot be modified or deleted until a retention period expires — even by administrators with root credentials. Compliance regulations like SEC Rule 17a-4 (broker-dealer records), HIPAA (medical records), SOX (financial controls), and FINRA (broker communications) mandate that records be retained immutably for 3–7 years, with no possibility of tampering — because the regulator's audit assumes the data has not been altered by an insider covering tracks. S3 Object Lock provides WORM in two modes: **Compliance Mode** (retention period cannot be shortened or removed by anyone, including root — the only way out is waiting) and **Governance Mode** (privileged users can override, useful for testing). Glacier Vault Lock provides similar immutability at the vault level — once a vault lock policy is written, it cannot be changed, and all objects in the vault inherit it. Legal holds are a separate mechanism: a binary flag on an object that prevents deletion indefinitely until the hold is released, typically used during litigation or investigation. The trade-off of WORM is operational rigidity — if you lock a wrong object or set the wrong retention, you cannot undo it (Compliance Mode), so testing in Governance Mode first is essential. The cost of WORM is minimal (no storage premium), but the operational discipline required is significant.
**Visual:**
```
WORM:       write once -> immutable -> no modify, no delete until retention expires
S3 Object Lock:
  Compliance mode:  root cannot override (strict, for SEC/HIPAA)
  Governance mode:  privileged users can override (testing/staging)
Glacier Vault Lock: vault-level policy, immutable once locked
Legal hold:        binary flag, blocks deletion until released (litigation)
```

### Q4. What is the cost trade-off between hot and cold storage, and when does archiving pay off?
**Answer:** The cost arithmetic of archiving is determined by four factors: storage cost per TB-month (Standard ~$23, IA ~$12.50, Glacier Flex ~$1, Deep ~$0.4), retrieval cost per GB ($0 for Standard, ~$0.01–0.10 for cold tiers), retrieval latency (ms for hot, hours for cold), and minimum storage duration (30d IA, 90d Glacier Flex, 180d Deep). Archiving pays off when (storage savings × time) > (retrieval fees × retrieval volume). Example: 100 TB of log data, accessed 1 TB/month via Athena queries. Hot storage cost: 100 × $23 = $2,300/month. Archive to Glacier Deep at 90 days: 25 TB hot (last 90d) + 75 TB deep = (25 × $23) + (75 × $0.4) = $575 + $30 = $605/month, plus retrieval of 1 TB × $0.03 = $30 retrieval fee. Total: $635/month, a 3.6x saving. Break-even: if retrieval exceeded ~55 TB/month, the retrieval fees would wipe out the storage savings. Archiving does NOT pay off when: (1) access frequency is high (retrieval fees dominate); (2) data is deleted before the minimum duration (early deletion fees apply); (3) the volume is small (operational complexity outweighs savings — don't archive 50 GB). Rule of thumb: archive when access drops below 1% of data per month and the retention is at least 6 months.
**Visual:**
```
storage $/TB-mo:   Hot $23 | IA $12.5 | Glacier $1 | Deep $0.4
retrieval $/GB:    Hot $0  | IA $0.01  | Glacier $0.03 | Deep $0.10
min duration:      Hot 0   | IA 30d    | Glacier 90d   | Deep 180d
breakeven:         (storage_savings x time) > (retrieval_fees x volume)
archive when:      access < 1% per month, retention >= 6 months
```

### Q5. How do you handle retrieval of archived data when the application needs it?
**Answer:** Retrieval of cold-tier data requires an asynchronous workflow because the latency is minutes-to-hours, not milliseconds. The pattern: (1) **Submit a restore request** via API (`RestoreObject` on S3 Glacier, `Rehydrate` on Azure Archive) specifying the retrieval tier (Standard 1-5 min, Bulk 5-12 hr, Expedited sub-minute for premium fee). (2) **Poll or wait for completion** — the storage service stages the object into a hot bucket (S3 Standard) for a temporary window (default 7 days) and sends an S3 event notification on completion. (3) **Read the staged copy** — once staged, reads are millisecond-latency from the hot bucket. (4) **Staging expires** — after the temporary window, the staged copy is removed (the archive remains in cold storage). For user-facing applications, the UX pattern is "request the restore, show the user a notification 'your file will be ready in 2 hours,' then notify them when ready" — common for archive-browsing UIs (Netflix's content archive portal, banking statement retrieval). For batch analytics (Athena, BigQuery), the workflow is "initiate a bulk restore of a partition, wait, then run the query" — typically orchestrated by Airflow. Anti-pattern: synchronously waiting on a Glacier retrieval in a request handler — the request will time out. Always decouple via a queue and notification. Cost optimization: use Bulk retrieval for large volumes (10x cheaper than Expedited) when the latency is acceptable.
**Visual:**
```
app -> RestoreObject(key, tier=Bulk) -> S3 Glacier (12 hr)
                                       |
                                       v  (event notification)
app <- "object staged in S3 Standard for 7 days" <- S3 event
app -> read from S3 Standard (ms latency) -> done
after 7 days: staged copy removed, archive remains in cold
UX: "file will be ready in 2 hr" -> notify user -> read
```

### Q6. What is data tiering inside a database, and how does it differ from archiving to object storage?
**Answer:** Database-native tiering (MongoDB Online Archive, Postgres tablespace on cold disk, Oracle Heat Map) automatically moves old partitions or rows to cheaper storage while keeping them queryable through the same database interface. The database handles the tier transparently — a query like `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE date < '2020'` automatically routes to the cold tier, returns results (slower, but no separate API). Archiving to object storage (Glacier, ADLS) removes the data from the database entirely — the data lives in a separate system, queries require either restoring back to the DB or running a separate engine (Athena, BigQuery external tables) against the object store. Trade-offs: database tiering is simpler operationally (one query interface, no separate restore workflow) but more expensive (the cold tier is still attached to a database node, often SSD-backed even if lower-tier); object storage archiving is dramatically cheaper (10–100x) but breaks the unified query model — analysts must know which system holds which data. The modern pattern is hybrid: keep the last 12-18 months in the operational database for sub-second analytics, push older data to a data lake (S3 + Parquet + Athena) for occasional historical queries, and archive to Glacier only for compliance retention where queries are extremely rare (audit, dispute). Tools like Snowflake's external tables and BigQuery's BigLake blur the line by making object storage queryable as if it were a database table.
**Visual:**
```
DB tiering:   old partitions stay IN database, on cold disk, transparent SQL
              simple ops, expensive storage, slower old-data queries
Object arch:  old data REMOVED from DB, lives in S3/Glacier, separate engine
              cheap storage, breaks unified query, needs restore workflow
hybrid:       12-18mo in DB (fast) -> 1-7yr in lake (Athena) -> 7yr+ in Glacier
              BigLake/Snowflake external tables blur the line
```

### Q7. How does GDPR's "right to be forgotten" interact with archiving and retention laws?
**Answer:** GDPR Article 17 grants individuals the right to request deletion of their personal data, but Article 17(3)(b) and (e) provide exceptions: deletion is not required where processing is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation (e.g., tax law requiring 7-year retention) or for the establishment, exercise, or defense of legal claims. This creates a fundamental tension: a bank cannot honor a GDPR deletion request for transaction records that SEC/SOX requires them to retain. The practical resolution is **legal hold plus partial deletion**: the bank deletes the customer's personal data from operational systems (CRM, marketing, support tickets) and pseudonymizes the retained records (replace `name`, `email`, `phone` with a hash or token) so the data no longer identifies the individual, while keeping the financial transaction records (now de-identified) for the regulatory retention period. For archived data on Glacier with Vault Lock, deletion is technically impossible until the retention expires — so the response to the GDPR request is "we have pseudonymized your records; full deletion will occur at the end of the legal retention period." The architecture requires: (1) a customer-data inventory mapping every system that holds PII; (2) pseudonymization tools that can scrub archives in place (challenging for immutable WORM storage — typically requires designing the archive to store already-pseudonymized data); (3) a DSAR (Data Subject Access Request) workflow that responds within 30 days. Anti-pattern: storing unencrypted PII in WORM-locked archives — there is no recovery path if a breach occurs.
**Visual:**
```
GDPR Art 17:     right to deletion  ->  EXCEPT legal retention (tax, SOX, HIPAA)
bank response:   delete from CRM/marketing (operational) -> immediate
                 pseudonymize transaction records (hash name/email/phone)
                 keep pseudonymized records until retention expires -> then delete
WORM archive:    must store ALREADY-pseudonymized data (cannot modify in place)
DSAR workflow:   30-day response, inventory-driven, partial-deletion pattern
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your S3 bill is $80K/month, 60% of which is for objects untouched in 6 months. What's your plan?
**Answer:** First, instrument with S3 Storage Lens to confirm the breakdown: which prefixes hold the cold data, what storage classes they're in, and what the access pattern looks like. Then design tiered lifecycle policies: (1) For prefixes with >90 days of inactivity (likely `logs/`, `media-archive/`, `snapshots/`), add a policy `Standard -> IA at 30d -> Glacier Flex at 90d -> Glacier Deep at 180d`. (2) For compliance-retained data (`audit-records/`, `trade-history/`), transition directly to Glacier Deep with Object Lock in Compliance mode for the regulatory retention period (e.g., 7 years). (3) For versioned buckets with many non-current versions, add a rule to delete non-current versions after 90 days. (4) For abandoned experimental data (`tmp/`, `staging/`), add an expiration rule at 30 days to encourage cleanup. Implement gradually: apply to one prefix at a time, monitor Storage Lens for 2 weeks to confirm transitions are happening and no application breaks (i.e., no surprise "Object is in Glacier" errors). Set up CloudWatch alarms for Glacier restore requests — if restores spike, the policy is too aggressive and needs adjustment. Communicate the change to application teams — any code reading S3 directly needs to handle `Object is in Glacier` errors gracefully by initiating a restore. Expected savings: 60% of $80K = $48K, transitioning at avg 25x cost reduction on cold data yields ~$46K saved, total bill drops to ~$34K. Timeline: 4 weeks to design and roll out, 1 month to see full effect as objects transition. Operational cost: minimal after setup, but expect some access errors during the first week as teams learn the restore workflow.
**Visual:**
```
instrument:  S3 Storage Lens -> confirm tier distribution + access pattern
policy 1:    logs/ -> IA 30d -> Glacier 90d -> Deep 180d -> expire 1y
policy 2:    audit/ -> Deep immediately + Object Lock Compliance 7y
policy 3:    versioned buckets -> expire non-current after 90d
policy 4:    tmp/staging/ -> expire 30d
roll out:    one prefix at a time, monitor 2w, alarm on restore spikes
expected:    $80K -> ~$34K (57% reduction)
```

### Q2. A financial regulator audits your transaction archive. How do you prove the data hasn't been tampered with?
**Answer:** The audit requires demonstrating immutability from ingestion through retention. Architecture: (1) **Ingestion immutability** — transactions land in an append-only Kafka topic, are written to S3 with Object Lock in Compliance mode (retention 7 years) within minutes of generation, and the original write is logged with a hash (SHA-256) of the record content. (2) **Storage immutability** — S3 Object Lock Compliance mode prevents any modification or deletion by anyone (including root) until retention expires; Vault Lock on Glacier archives provides the same guarantee at the vault level. (3) **Hash chain** — each record's SHA-256 is appended to a Merkle tree whose root is published daily to an external notarization service (or written to a separate WORM-locked log), creating a tamper-evident chain: any modification to a historical record would break the hash chain. (4) **Audit log** — every access (read, restore, lifecycle transition, governance-mode attempt) is logged to CloudTrail and itself stored in a WORM-locked bucket. For the audit: provide the regulator with a sample of records, their hashes, the Merkle proof to the notarized root, the CloudTrail access log showing no modification attempts, and the Object Lock retention configuration. Run a verification job that recomputes hashes for a sample of records and confirms they match the chain. The regulator can independently verify by recomputing the SHA-256 of any record and comparing. Anti-pattern: relying on a database's "audit log" alone — if an insider can modify the database, they can modify the audit log too. The immutability must be enforced at the storage layer (Object Lock) AND verified cryptographically (hash chain).
**Visual:**
```
ingest:    txn -> Kafka (append-only) -> S3 + Object Lock Compliance 7y
           hash(txn) -> Merkle tree -> root notarized daily
storage:   Object Lock Compliance: root cannot delete until 7y expires
           Glacier Vault Lock: vault-level immutable policy
verify:    sample records -> recompute SHA-256 -> match Merkle chain
audit:     CloudTrail log (WORM-locked) -> no modification attempts
           provide regulator: hashes, Merkle proofs, retention config
anti:      DB audit log alone = insider can modify both DB and log
```

### Q3. You need to run a one-time analysis on 5 years of archived order data currently in Glacier Deep. How do you do it cost-effectively?
**Answer:** Restoring 5 years (say, 50 TB) from Glacier Deep is expensive ($0.10/GB retrieval = $5,000) and slow (12 hours per restore batch). The cost-effective approach: (1) **Use Bulk retrieval tier** — $0.025/GB instead of $0.10 (Standard), saving 75%. Bulk has 48-hour latency but for batch analysis that's fine. (2) **Restore to S3 Standard as Parquet** — initiate `RestoreObject` on each archive with `Tier=Bulk` and `Days=30` (staging window). Use S3 Batch Operations to orchestrate the restore of all 50 TB in parallel, completing in 48 hours. (3) **Run Athena queries against the staged Parquet** — Athena charges $5/TB scanned, so scanning 50 TB costs $250, but with partition pruning (filter by year/month) you can scan only the relevant 5-10 TB for ~$25-50. (4) **Materialize aggregates** — instead of repeatedly scanning the cold data, run the analysis once, write the aggregated results to a small S3 Standard bucket, then delete the staged restore (let it expire after 30 days or initiate early deletion if minimum duration is met). (5) **Consider alternative: BigQuery external tables on Coldline** — if the data is already in GCP, BigQuery can query Coldline directly with no restore step, paying only per-byte scanned (similar cost, no 48-hour wait). Total cost: $1,250 retrieval (Bulk) + $50 Athena scan + $30 staging storage = ~$1,330, vs $5,000+ for Standard retrieval and re-ingestion. Timeline: 48 hours for restore, then queries run in minutes. For recurring analysis, materialize daily/weekly aggregates back to a hot tier so subsequent queries don't re-scan the cold data.
**Visual:**
```
restore:    50 TB from Glacier Deep, Bulk tier ($0.025/GB = $1,250, 48 hr)
            S3 Batch Operations orchestrates parallel restore
stage:      -> S3 Standard (Parquet, partitioned by year/month), 30d window
query:      Athena on staged Parquet, partition pruning -> scan 5-10 TB ($25-50)
materialize: aggregates -> small S3 Standard bucket (cheap, fast repeat queries)
expire:     let staged copy expire (or early-delete if min duration met)
alt:        BigQuery external table on Coldline -> query directly, no restore
total:      $1,330 vs $5,000+ for Standard retrieval + re-ingest
```

### Q4. Your application experiences latency spikes when users access archived documents. How do you fix it?
**Answer:** The latency spike is because archived documents require a synchronous restore (minutes to hours) that the application is exposing to users. The fix has two parts: UX and architecture. (1) **UX fix** — when a user requests an archived document, immediately respond with a notification "this document is being retrieved from archive, you'll receive an email in ~2 hours" rather than blocking the request. Track the restore request in a queue (SQS), initiate the restore via the storage API, and notify the user via email/push when the staged copy is ready. (2) **Predictive pre-staging** — analyze access patterns: if a user viewing their account page frequently clicks "view historical statements," pre-stage the most recent 12 months of statements on-demand when they log in (cheap if it's <1 GB total). For frequently-accessed archives (top 1% by access count), keep a hot cache in S3 Standard with a TTL of 7 days. (3) **Two-tier architecture** — split the archive into "warm archive" (Glacier Instant Retrieval, ms latency, $0.004/GB-month) for documents likely to be accessed, and "deep archive" (Glacier Deep, 12 hr, $0.00099/GB-month) for the long tail. Move documents to warm archive when an access pattern indicates likely future access (e.g., a customer opens a support ticket -> pre-stage their last 6 months of records). (4) **Restore prioritization** — use Expedited retrieval (1-5 min, $0.10/GB premium) for user-initiated requests, Bulk (5-12 hr, $0.025/GB) for batch pre-staging. (5) **Monitor and alert** — track restore latency and volume; if Expedited restores exceed quota, you may need to provision more capacity. Anti-pattern: synchronous restore in the request path — always decouple via async workflow with notification.
**Visual:**
```
bad:        user clicks doc -> sync RestoreObject -> 12 hr block -> timeout
good:       user clicks doc -> "we'll email you in 2 hr" -> SQS -> restore -> notify
predictive: user logs in -> pre-stage recent 12mo docs to warm cache (TTL 7d)
two-tier:   warm archive (Glacier Instant, ms, $0.004/GB) for likely-accessed
            deep archive (Glacier Deep, 12hr, $0.00099/GB) for long tail
priority:   Expedited (1-5 min, $0.10/GB) for user requests
            Bulk (5-12 hr, $0.025/GB) for batch pre-staging
```

### Q5. You're designing a system that must retain 7 years of audit logs for compliance but also support occasional search. What's the architecture?
**Answer:** The architecture separates the immutable retention layer (cold, cheap, WORM) from the searchable index layer (warm, queryable, derived). (1) **Ingestion** — audit logs stream into Kafka, are written to S3 with Object Lock in Compliance mode (7-year retention) as newline-delimited JSON, partitioned by `date/service/severity`. This is the immutable retention layer — Glacier Deep tier via lifecycle policy after 30 days, costs ~$0.4/TB-month. (2) **Index layer** — as logs land, a streaming job (Kinesis Firehose, Flink) extracts key fields (timestamp, user_id, event_type, request_id, severity) and writes them to OpenSearch (for full-text search) and a Postgres/Redshift table (for structured queries). The index is small (~1% of raw log size) and lives on hot storage. (3) **Search workflow** — analyst queries the index ("show me all admin actions on user X in 2021") and gets back matching record IDs and metadata. If they need the full log content, the index entry includes the S3 object key and byte offset; a Bulk restore is initiated (or the record is in Glacier Instant Retrieval for ms access), and the full content is returned within minutes. (4) **Aggregates** — pre-compute daily/weekly/monthly summaries (event counts by type, top users by action) into a small fact table — most compliance queries hit the aggregates, not the raw logs. (5) **Retention** — index and aggregates are retained for 7 years alongside the raw logs; both are deleted together at end of retention. (6) **Cost** — for 1 TB/month of audit logs (84 TB over 7 years), Glacier Deep storage costs ~$34/month, index (~10 GB/month) on OpenSearch costs ~$500/month, aggregates (~1 GB/month) on Redshift negligible. Total: ~$534/month vs ~$1,932/month for keeping raw logs in Standard.
**Visual:**
```
ingest:     Kafka -> S3 + Object Lock Compliance 7y (JSON, partitioned)
                       |
                       v (lifecycle: Glacier Deep at 30d)
retention:  WORM immutable, ~$0.4/TB-mo, full content (84 TB over 7y)
            |
            +--> streaming extract -> index layer (small, hot)
                 OpenSearch: timestamp, user, event_type (1% of raw size)
                 Redshift: daily/weekly aggregates (top events, counts)
search:     analyst -> query index -> record IDs + S3 key + offset
                 -> restore from Glacier (Bulk, minutes) -> full content
cost:       $34/mo (raw) + $500/mo (OpenSearch) + ~$0 (aggregates) = $534/mo
vs:        $1,932/mo for raw in S3 Standard
```

### Q6. Your team accidentally archived the wrong prefix and broke production. How do you recover and prevent recurrence?
**Answer:** First, recover: (1) Identify the scope — which objects were transitioned and to which tier. (2) Initiate a restore of the affected objects from Glacier back to S3 Standard. For Glacier Flexible Retrieval, use Expedited (1-5 min, $0.10/GB) for user-facing data, Standard for less urgent. For Glacier Deep Archive, even Expedited is 12 hours — there is no faster option. (3) While restore runs, switch the application to read from a backup or replica if available. (4) Once restored, copy the objects back to S3 Standard permanently (a restore only stages a temporary copy — the archive remains in cold storage). Use `aws s3 cp s3://bucket/key s3://bucket/key --storage-class STANDARD` to overwrite the storage class. (5) Update the lifecycle policy to exclude the affected prefix and verify no further transitions occur. Prevention: (1) **Policy review process** — any lifecycle policy change requires peer review and a dry-run on a test prefix for 2 weeks before production. (2) **Canary deployment** — apply new policies to a small prefix (`logs/test/`) first, verify transitions match expectations, then expand. (3) **Tag-based policies** — instead of prefix-based, use S3 tags (`archive=true`) and apply policy only to tagged objects, so adding a tag is a deliberate act per object. (4) **Monitoring** — alert on unexpected Glacier restore volume (spike = something is reading archived data, possibly broken). (5) **IAM separation** — only a dedicated `lifecycle-manager` role can modify lifecycle policies, not application teams. (6) **Documentation** — maintain a runbook per prefix explaining what data lives there, who owns it, and what lifecycle applies. Post-mortem: the lesson is that lifecycle policies are infrastructure-as-code — they need the same change management discipline as database migrations.
**Visual:**
```
recover:    identify scope -> restore from Glacier (Expedited 1-5 min, $0.10/GB)
            Glacier Deep: 12 hr minimum, no faster option
            copy back to STANDARD (restore only stages temp copy)
            update policy to exclude prefix, verify no more transitions
prevent:    peer review + 2-week dry-run on test prefix before prod
            canary: small prefix first, verify, then expand
            tag-based policy: only tagged objects transition (deliberate per object)
            alert: Glacier restore volume spike = something broken
            IAM: only lifecycle-manager role can modify policies
            runbook per prefix: owner, data, lifecycle applied
```

### Q7. A media company has 10 PB of original footage, 2 PB accessed monthly, the rest rarely. Design the storage architecture.
**Answer:** A three-tier architecture matching the access pattern: (1) **Hot tier (2 PB, S3 Standard)** — the 20% accessed monthly, including current productions, in-progress edits, and the last 90 days of new footage. Storage: 2 PB × $23/TB = $46,000/month. Reads: ms latency, no retrieval fees. (2) **Warm archive (3 PB, S3 Standard-IA)** — footage from 90 days to 2 years, accessed occasionally for re-edits, trailers, marketing. Storage: 3 PB × $12.5/TB = $37,500/month. Reads: ms latency, $0.01/GB retrieval (rare access, low cost). (3) **Cold archive (5 PB, S3 Glacier Deep Archive with Vault Lock)** — footage older than 2 years, accessed only for remasters or legal holds. Storage: 5 PB × $0.4/TB = $2,000/month. Reads: 12-hour latency, $0.10/GB retrieval (rare, planned). (4) **Lifecycle policy** — `Standard -> IA at 90d -> Glacier Deep at 730d (2y) -> expire at 30y` (or never, depending on rights). (5) **Metadata layer** — a Postgres table holds the catalog (asset ID, title, shoot date, location, S3 key, current tier, access count), queryable in ms. Editors browse the catalog, request a restore, get notified when ready. (6) **CDN for delivered content** — finalized deliverables (mastered MP4s, trailers) live on hot tier + CloudFront CDN for distribution to viewers; only the source footage and intermediates are archived. (7) **Backup** — all tiers replicated cross-region (S3 cross-region replication) for DR. Total monthly cost: ~$85,500 + retrieval fees (~$2K/month typical) + metadata DB (~$1K) + CDN (~$5K) = ~$93K/month. Compared to keeping everything on Standard ($230K/month), saves ~$137K/month. Key insight: the metadata catalog is the access path — make it fast and complete, so users rarely need to look at the raw archive index.
**Visual:**
```
hot (2 PB, S3 Standard):       current + last 90d, $46K/mo, ms access
warm (3 PB, S3 Standard-IA):   90d-2y, $37.5K/mo, ms + $0.01/GB
cold (5 PB, Glacier Deep):     2y+, $2K/mo, 12hr + $0.10/GB, Vault Lock
lifecycle:                     Standard -> IA 90d -> Deep 730d -> expire/keep 30y
metadata:                      Postgres catalog (asset ID, title, S3 key, tier, accesses)
                              editors browse catalog -> request restore -> notify
deliverables:                  mastered MP4s on hot + CloudFront CDN (separate from archive)
DR:                            cross-region replication on all tiers
total:                         ~$93K/mo vs ~$230K all-hot (saves $137K/mo)
```
